q: Which airway problem is typical of acromegaly?
o: Large tongue, thick pharyngeal tissue and laryngeal stenosis making mask ventilation and intubation difficult
why: Acromegaly enlarges lips, tongue and jaw, thickens pharyngeal tissue and can narrow the larynx; OSA is common.

q: Which test is used to diagnose Cushing’s syndrome?
why: Late-night salivary cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression or 24-hour urinary free cortisol.

q: After pituitary surgery a patient passes over 300 ml/h of dilute urine and the serum sodium is 150 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Cranial DI causes large volumes of dilute urine and hypernatraemia; treat with desmopressin (DDAVP) and replace fluid.

q: Which hyponatraemic condition after neurosurgery is treated with fluid restriction?
why: SIADH is euvolaemic and treated with fluid restriction; cerebral salt wasting is hypovolaemic and treated with sodium and fluid replacement.

q: How can the anaesthetist help the pituitary descend into the surgical field?
o: Allowing a raised PaCO2 or injecting saline via a lumbar drain
why: Raising PaCO2 (or ICP via a lumbar drain) brings the gland down; Valsalva tests for a CSF leak.

q: Why is extubation done awake after transsphenoidal surgery?
o: Nasal packs mean the patient must mouth-breathe and protect their airway
It is not: deep extubation is standard
why: Nasal packs block the nose; an awake, smooth extubation reduces the risk of obstruction.

q: Which drug used on the nasal mucosa can cause hypertension and arrhythmias during transsphenoidal surgery?
why: Cocaine and adrenaline-containing nasal preparations cause hypertension and tachyarrhythmias.

q: Which visual field defect is classic for a pituitary tumour compressing the chiasm?
why: Compression of the optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia.

q: Which hormone is produced by the posterior pituitary?
why: The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin; the anterior lobe releases ACTH, GH, FSH, LH, TSH and prolactin.
